Transcript body:
[00:00:00] Jillian: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, this is Jillian from Redwood marketing. Today we're recording a short interview about Starry Health's patient support flow and how Redwood fits in. Quick audio note — we'll edit any bits, okay?
[00:00:12] Dr. Ana: Yep that's fine, thanks. 
[00:00:17] Kelvin: We're good on our side. A few people in the room listening.
[00:00:24] Jillian: Great. Marcus is here too, our SE, he'll jump in for the tech bits. Marcus — quick intro?
[00:00:30] Marcus: Hey all, Marcus Lee, solutions engineer at Redwood. I work on dedicated and private deployments, bench runs, you know the fun stuff.
[00:00:41] Rina: I'm Rina, product marketing at Starry, I'm going to help shepherd the case study approval.
[00:00:47] Jillian: Cool. So maybe Ana — can you set the scene, what was the user problem you were solving?
[00:00:54] Dr. Ana: Yeah so for us patient support — we handle triage questions, appointment changes, medication clarifications — it was all this steady stream of short messages. Historically we had an in-house model pipeline running on CPUs, latencies were inconsistent, costs spiked when volume hit, and we couldn't guarantee PHI isolation. That meant long manual processes.
[00:01:20] Kelvin: Right, we also had concerns about auditability and retention for medical data, and the infra ops burden got heavy.
[00:01:29] Jillian: And where did Redwood first come into the picture?
[00:01:33] Dr. Ana: We saw Redwood on a benchmark doc — the latency profiles looked good, and the suggestion of dedicated pools for regulated data was what sold it. We started a small pilot.
[00:01:46] Marcus: To add, the pilot was focused on two flows: short triage replies and a longer follow-up summarization task. For the triage we used a quantized open model, and for summarization we pinned a larger variant.
[00:01:58] Jillian: Can you share numbers from the pilot? Folks love metrics.
[00:02:03] Dr. Ana: Yeah, caveat — these are early numbers, but we saw median latency for the triage path move from ~650 ms on our old infra to ~220 ms on Redwood Dedicated. Cost per interaction dropped, roughly we saw a 38% reduction in inference cost after enabling batching and prefix caching.
[00:02:27] Kelvin: I remember the first week — we were skeptical of batching because of latency guarantees, but Redwood's SLO knobs let us tune batch size vs max latency and we hit our targets.
[00:02:39] Marcus: There was also the KV cache for common prefixes — that saved a surprising amount for repeat prompts.
[00:02:46] Rina: From a product POV that meant we could route lower-risk tasks to cheaper variants and still keep the critical stuff on pinned models.
[00:02:55] Jillian: Excellent. Security came up in prep notes — please talk through the path you chose for PHI.
[00:03:01] Dr. Ana: We opted for Redwood Private initially — VPC with customer-managed KMS. We needed complete control over keys and audit logs. The Redwood team helped map audit events to our SIEM. SOC2 evidence and SSO integrations were also requested and provided.
[00:03:20] Kelvin: The HSM/KMS details were important — we run quarterly audits and the binder of logs Redwood provided made the first audit much easier.
[00:03:30] Marcus: We also set up RBAC so only the triage model service had decrypt permissions; human reviewers are a separate role.
[00:03:37] Dr. Ana: Small transcription glitch — for the record, the security docs were thorough but we did ask a few follow-up questions about retention windows. Redwood answered that with config for retention-by-route.
[00:03:49] Jillian: Nice. Any surprises during the rollout?
[00:03:53] Kelvin: The main surprise was how quickly we could iterate on prompts once latency stabilized; product got faster feedback so we increased automation scope. Performance stability reduced manual QA time.
[00:04:07] Dr. Ana: Another small thing — model quantization across requests had slightly different tokenization in edge cases, we had to tweak prompt templates, but Marcus helped with guidelines.
[00:04:18] Marcus: Yeah I sent a notes doc and a small checklist: tokenization checks, warm-up policy for cold caches, and a recommended canary policy.
[00:04:27] Rina: That checklist is gold for us marketing-wise too because we can turn it into a short best-practices snip for the case study.
[00:04:34] Jillian: Ok let's pivot to the podcast/story — how should we frame the result? Quotes? Numbers?
[00:04:40] Dr. Ana: Feel free to use the latency and cost numbers I gave, and I'd like a quote about the operational impact: something like, "We went from firefighting infra to iterating on product features — Redwood made that possible."
[00:04:58] Rina: Also call out PHI compliance and auditability as a key decision factor.
[00:05:05] Jillian: We'll draft two short quote options and circulate. We'll also produce an edited audio clip for social. Any concerns about regulatory wording?
[00:05:14] Kelvin: Just be careful not to imply Redwood stores PHI outside our managed VPC — that's important. Keep it clear we control keys and retention.
[00:05:24] Jillian: Noted. Marcus, can you confirm the artifacts we'll share after this call?
[00:05:28] Marcus: Yep — I'll share latency/cost charts from the pilot, the SOC2 summary and the checklist I mentioned. I'll also attach a short runbook for canarying model changes.
[00:05:39] Dr. Ana: Quick side — the triage bot's CSAT went up a bit. We track satisfaction on quick replies, that's improved from 72% to about 82% since the pilot.
[00:05:50] Rina: Nice metric. That, plus latency, makes a good narrative: faster replies, happier patients, lower cost.
[00:05:59] Jillian: Any competitors or alternate vendors you evaluated?
[00:06:02] Kelvin: We ran a short bench vs Anthropic and an in-house optimized pipeline. Anthropic did well on safety demos but cost and lack of private deployment was a blocker. Our in-house stack lacked scalability.
[00:06:16] Marcus: Redwood's hybrid offering — dedicated pools + private control plane — was the differentiator for them.
[00:06:22] Dr. Ana: Agreed.
[00:06:25] Jillian: Okay, logistics for the case study: we'll draft copy, send to Rina and Ana for approval, and include two graphics (latency graph, cost-per-interaction). Anything else?
[00:06:34] Rina: If you can include a small timeline of the pilot (dates and key milestones) that's helpful.
[00:06:40] Marcus: I'll add a short appendix with experiment config: model names used, quantization, batch sizes.
[00:06:46] Jillian: Great. Are there any off-the-record comments or do-not-publish bits?
[00:06:51] Dr. Ana: We asked not to publish raw logs or exact retention policies, but aggregated metrics are fine.
[00:06:58] Jillian: Understood. We'll respect that.
[00:07:02] Rina: One more marketing ask — can we get a 15–30s highlight clip suitable for LinkedIn?
[00:07:08] Jillian: Absolutely. We'll cut an audio highlight and a short quote card.
[00:07:13] Kelvin: Also please include the contact for our privacy team for legal approval, I can loop them in if needed.
[00:07:20] Jillian: Please do. We'll include a review step in the workflow.
[00:07:24] -- audio markers and a couple minutes of informal chit-chat (off-topic: holiday plans) omitted by editor --
[00:22:40] Marcus: Back on track — I'm going to summarize the tech takeaways for the case study draft: 1) dedicated GPU pools reduced median triage latency 2) batching + prefix caching cut per-interaction cost ~38% 3) private VPC + KMS satisfied audit requirements and simplified compliance 4) tokenization quirks required minor prompt tweaks.
[00:22:59] Dr. Ana: That sounds accurate.
[00:23:05] Jillian: Final quick recap and next steps?
[00:23:09] Dr. Ana: We'll approve the quote and share any legal notes by the 15th.
[00:23:14] Rina: I will review copy and confirm the clip.
[00:23:18] Marcus: I'll send artifacts and the SOC2 summary by the 8th.
[00:23:22] Jillian: I'll deliver edited audio and transcript by the 10th, and a first draft of the case study next week.
[00:23:28] Kelvin: That's it from us, thanks everyone.
[00:23:32] Jillian: Thanks so much, we'll follow up by email with links to the draft and audio.
